newsitem.title: POLAND: Bank unlikely to save Poland's Gdansk shipyard.
newsitem.headline: Bank unlikely to save Poland's Gdansk shipyard.

text.p: Poland's bankrupt Gdansk shipyard, cradle of the Solidarity union movement that helped bring down the former communist government, appeared to be heading for collapse Wednesday as a local bank said it was unlikely to grant the enterprise a crucial loan.

The loan, of between $120 and $150 million, would have kept part of the yard's 5,000-member workforce busy building five vessels for a German investor while the government and the yard continued to seek an investor to save the business.

The German offer to sign a contract with the yard expires Thursday and without it the shipyard, operating under bankruptcy regulations since August with debts of 415 million zlotys ($148 million), would have little to do.
The workers, who suspended a protest campaign against the state-controlled yard's collapse last week, will receive wages from a special government fund until mid-February.

Bank Gdanski, with which the firm's administrator has been trying to negotiate the loan, said Wednesday that current cooperation on a contract to build one vessel had been unsatisfactory and had discouraged the bank from further deals with the shipyard.
The government reiterated on Wednesday that the only way it could help the shipyard was through extending partial credit guarantees, but only if a bank first agreed to a loan.
"If the government receives an application for guarantees, it will consider it," government spokeswoman Aleksandra Jakubowska told a news conference.

But the yard's administrator, Wieslaw Szaj, said he still thought the treasury, a bank and the yard could set up a temporary venture that would keep business alive during the hunt for a strategic investor.
